investigations.hypothesis: The postponed request is released only on the MsgAppResp commit path (raft.go:1550-1554), so a commit performed inside switchToConfig (raft.go:2013-2028) satisfies the release condition (newApplied >= pendingConfIndex is not involved; committedEntryInCurrentTerm() becomes true) without releasing it, leaving the received request unanswered until an unrelated commit or a client retry.
investigations.discriminator: Whether the omission has consequences beyond the unanswered caller - for example an application that ties its own deadline to the read and re-issues it, or a caller that reuses one request context for several reads - and whether the postponed form exists for any read-only option other than ReadOnlySafe.

Postponed requests are released only from the MsgAppResp commit path.
switchToConfig can perform the term's first commit and does not release pendingReadIndexMessages.

The applied progress report and the ApplyConfChange call are not ordered by the library's contract.

The Node.ReadIndex contract tells callers that read index requests can be lost without notice and that retries are their duty (node.go:218-224), so a retrying client is not blocked; the observation is an unanswered admissible request rather than a permanent client-visible outage.

The reachable prefix relies on documented application latitude - reporting applied progress before finishing the entries of a previous Ready (node.go:166-178) and calling ApplyConfChange later than that report (node.go:179-187) - and this receipt shows that sequence is reachable through the public interface, so the premise no longer depends on a supplied fixture; the unanswered request is not caus [preview: 59 characters omitted; see full record]
limitations: The comparison holds the applied configuration change to be the one that first makes a current-term entry committable; a leader that had already committed any entry of its term answers later requests normally (committedEntryInCurrentTerm() is true, so nothing is postponed).

The public-contract harness drives the wrapped leader against bare raft followers, so the followers' Ready/Advance duties are exercised only implicitly (their acknowledgements are delivered or held by the harness) and both run in one process.

No state machine was run, so the consequence measured is the unanswered request itself (no ReadState, no MsgReadIndexResp). The safe-but-late index of the eventual answer follows from the contract, not from a served value in the receipt.

investigations.hypothesis: tracker.IsSingleton() only checks that the configuration has one voter, and stepLeader answers MsgReadIndex locally whenever it is true. latest_interpretation.rationale: Five receipts now cover the same removal in five configurations, and none of them produces the safe outcome the question allows. Source side: tracker.IsSingleton is a size test whose comment asserts that the single voting member is the leader (tracker/tracker.go:158-162); stepLeader's MsgReadIndex case answers from that test without a round (raft.go:1354-1361) and otherwise takes the read-only pat [preview: 3178 characters omitted; see full record]

knowledge.assertion: IsSingleton is a size-only test over the configuration and never compares the single voter with the local node.
StepLeader answers MsgReadIndex locally whenever IsSingleton holds, using its own commit index and without a round.
A removed leader keeps leading by default while its proposals are refused and its read answers are not.
Lease-based reads force CheckQuorum, and the lease makes voters refuse higher-term vote requests while they still hear the leader.

counterevidence: The controls hold in the singleton receipts (parsed index 4 of 8090da09e0d44e13af56696a62f13d45, parsed index 5 of 815614d02b874bc8b0661039ae0552da): the node that is the configuration's voter answers its own read with an index that covers its commit index, so the defect is the answering node's membership, not the singleton answer itself.

The CheckQuorum multi-voter receipt hands out no stale index: no new leader exists there and no entry is committed behind the removed leader's back (both committed indices are 2), so what the receipt shows is that the answering round counted the removed leader's own acknowledgement - a confirmation defect, not yet a stale read.

The same receipt's setup event still carries the field prevote:true, a label copied from the PreVote harness the file was derived from; the executed configuration set Config.CheckQuorum=true and left PreVote false, as the scope of the fixed experiment states.
limitations: Every scenario needs an application that applies the committed change removing the leading node while Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false and keeps that node running; applications that set the option, or that stop the removed node, do not reach the state.

The witnesses are at the ReadIndex contract level: the receipts show the index handed to the reader (locally or across the wire), or the request disappearing, or a round that counted a non-member - no state machine was run, so a served value that misses an entry is a consequence of the contract rather than a measured value.

The tick ratio is one heartbeat tick against ten election ticks in all five configurations; the multi-voter CheckQuorum receipt delivers no ticks to the voters, so the length of that exposure is unbounded within the receipt.

knowledge.assertion: The proposal channel is closed by the removal guard and restored only by a leadership change with a leader known.
With a nil proposal channel Propose blocks until the caller's context or the node's done channel fires.
Only a removal closes the channel; a demotion keeps the Progress entry and an addition never re-opens it.

knowledge.conditions: StateLeader with a non-empty voter set; called from applyConfChange (application applies a committed configuration change) with the leader's Progress values already reflecting quorum-level acknowledgement of a current-term entry.
